heat-physiology.title: How the Body Responds to Heat
heat-physiology.content: When the body begins to overheat, it responds by increasing blood flow to the skin to dissipate heat and by producing sweat. Sweat evaporation removes heat from the body surface. As heat exposure continues and the body struggles to cool itself, the heart rate increases, the core temperature rises, and performance can decline. If the body's cooling mechanisms are overwhelmed, heat-related illness can develop quickly. Workers must recognize that physical exertion in hot environments places an additional burden on the cardiovascular system.

dehydration-electrolytes.title: Dehydration and Electrolyte Loss
dehydration-electrolytes.content: Sweating removes both water and electrolytes (minerals such as sodium and potassium) from the body. In hot conditions, workers can lose large amounts of fluids rapidly. Thirst is not a reliable early warning — by the time thirst is felt, mild dehydration may already be present. Workers must drink water regularly throughout the shift, not just when thirsty. When heavy sweating occurs over extended periods, electrolyte replacement through sports drinks or food may also be needed to prevent muscle cramps and other heat-related conditions.

heat-illness-types.title: Types of Heat-Related Illness
heat-illness-types.content: Heat cramps are painful muscle cramps that occur after heavy sweating and electrolyte loss — typically in the legs or abdomen. They are an early warning that the body is struggling. Heat exhaustion is a more serious condition characterized by weakness, dizziness, heavy sweating, nausea, headache, and dehydration. A worker with heat exhaustion must be moved to a cool area, rested, and hydrated. If heat exhaustion is not recognized and addressed, it can progress to heat stroke — a life-threatening emergency that requires immediate medical attention.

heat-stroke-emergency.title: Heat Stroke: A Medical Emergency
heat-stroke-emergency.content: Heat stroke occurs when the body's core temperature rises to dangerous levels and the cooling system fails. Signs include confusion, altered mental status, slurred speech, loss of coordination, hot and flushed skin, and in some cases the absence of sweating. Heat stroke can cause permanent organ damage or death. It is a medical emergency — call emergency medical services immediately. While waiting for help, cool the worker as quickly as possible: move them to shade or a cool area, apply cool water or ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin, and fan the worker.

acclimatization.title: Acclimatization and New Worker Safety
acclimatization.content: Acclimatization is the process of gradually exposing the body to heat so it can adapt and work more efficiently in hot environments. The body's ability to tolerate heat improves over 7 to 14 days of gradual exposure. New workers, workers returning after illness or time away, and workers during early heat waves are at significantly higher risk because they have not yet acclimatized. Employers should schedule acclimatization periods with reduced workloads and more frequent breaks before transitioning workers to full exposure. Workers with medical conditions or who take certain medications may be at additional risk.

clothing-controls.title: Clothing Choices and Engineering Controls
clothing-controls.content: Clothing significantly affects heat burden. Loose, lightweight, breathable fabrics allow better air circulation and sweat evaporation. Dark, tight, or heavy clothing increases heat retention. When PPE must be worn, it can substantially increase heat load — additional monitoring and rest breaks may be required. Engineering controls that reduce heat stress include fans, ventilation systems, air conditioning in rest areas, radiant heat shields, shading for outdoor work, and cooling stations. Administrative controls include scheduling heavy work during cooler hours, rotating tasks, providing adequate rest breaks, and pairing workers to monitor each other for symptoms.

prevention-response.title: Prevention Strategies and Emergency Response
prevention-response.content: Preventing heat illness requires a combination of approaches: drink water regularly (approximately one cup every 15–20 minutes in heat); take breaks in shaded or air-conditioned rest areas; acclimatize new or returning workers; monitor coworkers for symptoms; use available engineering controls; dress appropriately for conditions; and know the emergency response plan. Workers must report symptoms such as dizziness, weakness, nausea, cramps, or unusual confusion promptly — early intervention prevents progression to heat stroke. All workers should know where emergency contacts, cool rest areas, and water stations are located.
